# Multiple reflected pairs at one actual fiber: allocation and saturation

These are sufficient conditions at one fixed integer fiber. They do not assert that an arbitrary mixed-integer body has a fiber satisfying them. The multiple-pair cap inequality uses each endpoint only once. The new saturation estimate allows the sum of midpoint densities to exceed one.

## 1. Actual reflected pairs and their simultaneous cap budget

Let `n>=1,d>=1`, let `C` be a convex body, and use its actual positive-volume fibers `K_z`. Write `M=sum_z |K_z|`. Fix an integer base `p` whose fiber `K=K_p` has volume `k>0`. An unordered reflected pair is `{z,w}` with `z!=w`, `z+w=2p`, and both endpoint fibers positive. Distinct such pairs have disjoint endpoints: the partner of `z` is uniquely `2p-z`. No pair uses `p`.

For pair `j` put

`a_j=|K_z|, b_j=|K_w|, B_j=((a_j^(1/d)+b_j^(1/d))/2)^d`.

Choose a number `0<=t_j<=min(a_j,b_j)`. There is a coupling of the two measures `(t_j/a_j)1_(K_z) dx` and `(t_j/b_j)1_(K_w) dx` whose midpoint measure `eta_j` satisfies

`eta_j <= (t_j/B_j)1_K dx`,

`eta_j(K)=t_j`, and `integral x d eta_j=t_j(g_z+g_w)/2`.       (1)

Here the midpoint support is in the actual fiber `K` by convexity. To obtain the density constant directly, use the conditional triangular map between uniform endpoint probabilities, as proved in `accepted fact 486fe778f838d99d, f6641f09c19819a3`. Its positive own-coordinate derivatives have product `b_j/a_j`. If they are `s_i`, then

`product_i(1+s_i) >= [1+(product_i s_i)^(1/d)]^d`.

Indeed, the elementary symmetric sum of order `l` is at least `binom(d,l)(product s_i)^(l/d)` by AM-GM over all `l`-subsets. The midpoint Jacobian is thus at least `B_j/a_j`. Repeated one-dimensional substitution gives (1). No affine map of the integer coordinates is used.

Put

`eta=sum_j eta_j`, `T=sum_j t_j`, `L=sum_j t_j/B_j`,

`alpha=T/k`, `delta=L-alpha`, and `R=M-k-2T`.             (2)

We have `R>=0` because the endpoint fractions are at most one and no endpoint is reused. We have `eta<=L1_K dx`, and hence `delta>=0`. Equivalently, each `B_j<=k` follows from Brunn--Minkowski and actual midpoint containment.

The measure `rho=1_K dx+2 eta` has centroid

`g=[k g_K+sum_j t_j(g_z+g_w)]/(k+2T)`.

The point `Y=(p,g)` is in the interior of the actual fiber `K`: `rho` is supported in `K` and dominates its uniform measure. It is the centroid of an actual allocated mixed submeasure of mass `k+2T`, whose integer centroid is exactly `p`. It need not be the centroid of the whole original set.

For every closed ambient halfspace `H`, with trace `H_p` in the middle fiber, the affine midpoint identity gives

`eta_j(H_p) <= (t_j/a_j)|K_z intersect H_z|+(t_j/b_j)|K_w intersect H_w|`.

Summing and retaining the own fiber proves the simultaneous inequality

`mu(S intersect H) >= |K intersect H_p|+eta(H_p)`.         (3)

It holds for all oblique normals and all closed boundaries. Pairwise source disjointness is essential to this step.

## 2. An explicit capacity-one allocation

If `sum_j t_j/B_j<=1`, the all-dimensional dominated-centroid theorem in `candidate 660db01ed45063dd` applies directly to the sum `eta`. Therefore

`D_S(Y) > (3/4) Gamma_d (k+T)`.                          (4)

The strictness is uniform by the explicit surplus in that theorem. A pure-integer through-source cap captures the own fiber and one endpoint fraction from each pair, of mass at least `k+T`, so it also satisfies (4).

The best `T` certified by this volume-only constraint is an attained finite fractional knapsack. Sort `B_1>=...>=B_m`, put `m_j=min(a_j,b_j)` and `C_j=sum_(i<=j)m_i/B_i`. If `C_m<=1`, use every `t_j=m_j`. Otherwise let `j` be the first index with `C_j>=1`, fill all earlier pairs, set `t_j=B_j(1-C_(j-1))`, and set later masses to zero. To prove optimality, write `e_j=t_j/B_j`; the objective is `sum B_j e_j` under `sum e_j<=1` and `0<=e_j<=m_j/B_j`. Exchanging any available allocation from a smaller coefficient to an unfilled larger coefficient never decreases the objective, and gives the stated allocation after finitely many fills. Ties cause no problem.

In particular, `k+T>=4M/(3*2^n)` is a proved sufficient condition for OC at this actual point. The ordinary heavy-fiber condition `k>=M/2^n` can of course be used separately.

This capacity-one bound cannot itself cover every body. For the actual product `[-2,2] times K` with `n=1`, the original mass is `5k`. Even allowing every coupling rather than the scalar sufficient constraint, `eta<=1_K` forces `T<=k`. Thus the numerical certificate on the right of (4) is at most `3 Gamma_d k/2`, whereas the OC target is `5 Gamma_d k/2`. This is a limitation of that certificate, not a bound on the depth of its center or a counterexample to OC.

## 3. A general density ceiling and the exact quantile constraint

Now let `K` be any full-dimensional convex body, and let `eta<=L1_K dx` have mass `alpha |K|`, where `L>=0` and `0<=alpha<=L`. Set `delta=L-alpha`, and let `g` be the centroid of `1_K+2 eta`. Normalize `|K|=1` temporarily. For a closed through-`g` halfspace with nonzero continuous normal, write `s=|K intersect H|` and `r=eta(H)`.

For the corresponding scalar projection, let `V(t)` be its cap-volume function. The root `V^(1/d)` is concave by actual cap inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski. Under uniform volume the random variable `V(X)` is uniform on `[0,1]`. The pushforward of `eta` has a density `h` with `0<=h<=L`, total mass `alpha`, and mass `r` on `[0,s]`. Jensen at the actual centroid gives

`(1+2alpha)s^(1/d) >= d/(d+1)+2 integral_0^1 v^(1/d)h(v)dv`. (5)

For `L>0`, minimizing that integral separately on the two intervals yields the exact necessary two-band constraint, with `q=1+1/d`,

`q(1+2alpha)s^(q-1) >= 1+2L^(1-q)r^q`

`                       +2L[s+(alpha-r)/L]^q-2L s^q`.    (6)

The status bounds are `max(0,alpha-L(1-s))<=r<=min(alpha,Ls)`. These conditions are necessary for actual bodies; no converse geometric realization is asserted.

A simpler explicit bound follows by placing all of the mass at the left endpoint of the whole quantile interval. Define

`b_d(L,alpha)=Gamma_d [(1+2L(alpha/L)^(1+1/d))/(1+2alpha)]^d`

for `L>0`, and `b_d(0,0)=Gamma_d`. Then

`s>=b_d(L,alpha)`,

`s+r >= b_d(L,alpha)+max(0,L b_d(L,alpha)-delta)`.         (7)

For the second statement use `r=Ls-zeta(H)>=Ls-delta`, where `zeta=L1_K-eta`, and also `r>=0`. The right side is increasing in `s`. Formula (7) is valid for arbitrary density ceiling, and retains both its total mass and its saturation deficit. It is exact at full saturation `eta=L1_K`: it gives `(1+L)Gamma_d`, attained by a simplex centroid vertex cap.

## 4. An explicit nonzero neighborhood of saturation

The following coarser bound has particularly simple exact consequences. Since `zeta=L1_K-eta` has mass `delta` and `0<=V^(1/d)<=1`, equation (5) gives

`s^(1/d) >= d/(d+1)-2delta/[(d+1)(1+2alpha)]`.

If `2delta<=d(1+2alpha)`, raise to the `d`-th power and use Bernoulli to obtain

`s >= Gamma_d [1-2delta/(1+2alpha)]`.

The right side is allowed to be negative, in which case the inequality is merely weaker. Combining with `r>=Ls-delta` gives

`s+r >= Gamma_d(1+L)[1-2delta/(1+2alpha)]-delta`.

Relative to half the allocated mixed mass, this is

`s+r >= (Gamma_d/2)(1+2alpha)+E_d(L,delta)`,               (8)

where

`E_d(L,delta)=Gamma_d/2-delta[1-Gamma_d+2Gamma_d(1+L)/(1+2L-2delta)]`.

Suppose now `L>=1` and `0<=delta<=1/8`. The condition for Bernoulli is automatic, and

`2(1+L)/(1+2L-2delta) <=16/11`.

Consequently

`E_d(L,delta) >=(39 Gamma_d-11)/88 >1/44`.                (9)

The last inequality uses `Gamma_d>1/3`, which follows from `Gamma_d>=1/e` and `e<3`. Both classical estimates also follow directly from `log(1+1/d)<1/d` and the exponential series.

There is a weaker version with no lower bound on `L`. If `delta<=1/8`, then `1+2alpha>=1` gives

`E_d(L,delta) >=(11 Gamma_d-4)/32 >0`,                    (10)

using `Gamma_d>4/11`, itself a consequence of `e<11/4`. Thus even a ceiling less than one can be treated by saturation rather than by the fixed `3/4` constant.

All these bounds are uniform over the continuous cap normal. Restoring the factor `k`, they give bounds on the infimum over such normals. For a pure-integer through-`Y` halfspace in the reflected-pair application, the allocated captured mass is at least `k+T=k(1+alpha)`. This is at least the right side of (8): its equivalent pre-subtraction expression is at most `(1+L)Gamma_d-delta<=1+alpha`. Likewise it is at least the right side of (7), since `b_d<=1` and the two possible expressions are bounded by `1` and `1+alpha`. Parallel inward translation handles every containing halfspace. Closed continuous boundaries are null, while pure-integer boundary fibers have been counted in full.

## 5. Original mass, unused fibers, and concrete tests

For the actual allocation in Section 1, let `u=R/k`. If the assumptions of (8) hold, a sufficient condition for the original OC target is

`u <= (2^(n-1)-1)(1+2alpha)+2^n E_d(L,delta)/Gamma_d`.      (11)

This follows by comparing the right side of (8) with `Gamma_d(1+2alpha+u)/2^n`; no mass is discarded from the denominator. In particular, when `L>=1,delta<=1/8`, the simpler condition

`u <= (2^(n-1)-1)(1+2alpha)+2^n/(44 Gamma_d)`              (12)

gives a strict improvement over OC. For `n=1`, the allowed unused mass is `R<=k/(22 Gamma_d)`; the dimension-independent sufficient version is `R<=k/11`, since `Gamma_d<=1/2`.

For a centrally symmetric complete lattice base with `2m+1` points and identical fiber `K`, use all `m` reflected pairs with full mass. Their identity couplings give `eta=m1_K`, so `L=alpha=m,delta=0`. The actual selected point is the centroid of `K` at the integer symmetry center. The bound is `(m+1)Gamma_d k`, exceeding `Gamma_d(2m+1)k/2` by `Gamma_d k/2`. Thus the saturation mechanism repairs the five-level limitation in Section 2.

More generally, there is an actual arbitrary-shape corollary. Suppose all positive fibers occur at a centrally symmetric set of bases about the integer `p`, with `m>=1` reflected pairs. Suppose pair `j` has equal endpoint volumes `v_j` (the endpoint shapes need not agree), and

`sum_j (1-v_j/k) <=1/8`.

Every summand is nonnegative by midpoint containment and Brunn--Minkowski. Choose the whole endpoint measures. Then `L=m`, `alpha=sum_j v_j/k`, `delta=sum_j(1-v_j/k)`, and `R=0`. The actual full mixed centroid has integer coordinate `p`, and (8)--(9) give

`D_S(Y) > Gamma_d M/2+k/44`.

Thus this corollary is a genuine finite-fiber theorem in every integer rank, with no condition on endpoint shapes or halfspace directions. Its stated volume-saturation condition is essential to the proof; it is not asserted for all centrally symmetric base configurations.

For the sharp base `{0,1}^n`, no two distinct bases have an integer midpoint that is again a selected vertex. At every actual base the pair family is empty, and the construction reduces to the ordinary own-fiber centroid. Its contribution is `Gamma_d k=M Gamma_d/2^n`, consistent with the sharp simplex product; no stronger assertion is made.

For the archived largest-parity obstruction `P=2 Delta_n intersect Z^n` with identical simplex fiber of volume `k`, every base is a vertex or an edge midpoint. A vertex has no distinct reflected pair. An edge midpoint has exactly one such pair, namely that edge's two vertices, since the edge is its minimal face. Thus the present mechanism gives at most the certificate `2 Gamma_d k` there; it does not charge the mass `(n+1)k` of the even parity class to one center. In this family the unused mass is explicitly `(|P|-3)k`, so the original-mass condition (11), rather than a parity-class shortcut, governs the sufficient test.

## 6. Retained limitations

The results require full-dimensional continuous fibers and `d>=1`. They do not identify an integer midpoint with the required saturation and unused-mass bounds for an arbitrary body. Nor do they permit combining pairs with different midpoints into a fictitious single fiber. The source allocation, output density ceiling, deterministic center, all ambient halfspaces, and original denominator are explicit; existence of a globally successful allocation remains a separate problem.
